title: First-Order Linear Equations
lead: A first-order linear differential equation can be put in the standard form y′ + p(x)y = q(x). Multiplying it by an integrating factor μ(x) turns its left-hand side into the derivative of a product, so both sides can be integrated; the method models a ball falling against air resistance and the current in an electric circuit.
objectives: Write a first-order linear differential equation in standard form.
Find an integrating factor and use it to solve a first-order linear differential equation.
Solve applied problems involving first-order linear differential equations.
summary_html:
• Any first-order linear differential equation can be written in the form $\kyprime+\kp(x)\kyfn=\kq(x).$
  • We can use a five-step problem-solving strategy for solving a first-order linear differential equation that may or may not include an initial value.
  • Applications of first-order linear differential equations include determining motion of a rising or falling object with air resistance and finding current in an electrical circuit.

exercises.prompt:
Are the following differential equations linear? Explain your reasoning.

$\kdydx=x^{2}\kyfn+\sin x$

answer.solution: Yes. Subtracting $x^{2}\kyfn$ from both sides gives $\kyprime-x^{2}\kyfn=\sin x,$ the form $a(x)\kyprime+b(x)\kyfn=c(x)$ with $a(x)=1,$ $b(x)=-x^{2}$ and $c(x)=\sin x.$

exercises.prompt:

Are the following differential equations linear? Explain your reasoning.

$\kdydt+\kyfn^{2}=x$

answer.solution: No. The term $\kyfn^{2}$ is not a function of the independent variable times $\kyfn,$ so the equation cannot be put in the form $a(x)\kyprime+b(x)\kyfn=c(x).$

True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

The differential equation $\kyprime=3x^{2}\kyfn-\cos(x)\kydprime$ is linear.

answer.solution: True. Rearranged, $\cos(x)\kydprime+\kyprime-3x^{2}\kyfn=0:$ every term is a function of $x$ times $\kyfn$ or one of its derivatives, so the equation is linear. It is of second order, though, so it is not one of the first-order linear equations $a(x)\kyprime+b(x)\kyfn=c(x)$ of this section.

exercises.prompt:
True or False? Justify your answer with a proof or a counterexample.

You can explicitly solve all first-order differential equations by separation or by the method of integrating factors.

answer.solution: False. A counterexample is $\kyprime=\kyfn^{2}+x:$ its right-hand side is not $f(x)g(\kyfn),$ so it is not separable, and since $\kyfn^{2}$ appears it is not linear, so neither separation of variables nor an integrating factor applies. Even a separable equation such as $\kyprime=e^{\kyfn^{2}}$ leads to an integral, $\int e^{-\kyfn^{2}}d\kyfn,$ with no elementary antiderivative, so $\kyfn$ cannot be found explicitly.
